title: Did Phones Crush 70% of Garmin's Business? So How Did Revenue Double｜Curio Files
description:
The story goes: free navigation on phones crushed 70% of Garmin's business. This episode opens its annual reports for fiscal 2008 through 2025 to see the day "could slow our growth" became "has caused our growth to stop," what happened to the phone it built itself, the other number it published that same day, and how many years revenue took to catch up.

"Crushed by phones" is marked as the popular version: the same reports also name built-in navigation in new cars, and 2009 also brought the recession and a price war. That phones stopped its growth is Garmin's own wording in its annual report. The Counterpoint smartwatch ranking covers only Q1 2022, as reported by 9to5Mac; the full-year figure of about $8.15 billion is the company's own forecast. The source of every number is listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the people and devices in them are generic cartoon designs, not real people or real products. This channel has no license or partnership with Garmin.

Data as of 2026-11-05

chapters.phone-callback: It built a phone of its own
chapters.turn-title: The other number that same day
chapters.close-answer: The empty spot on the windshield

t001.text: Ever used a navigator? Going somewhere new, you stuck it on the windshield.

t002.text: The company that sold the most of them worldwide is Garmin.

t003.text: In 2008, over 70% of its revenue came from car and portable navigation.

t004.text: Then phones got free navigation. All said: Garmin's crushed.

t005.text: But guess what: its fiscal 2025 revenue was over twice that year's.

t006.text: Stranger still: hunted by phones, it made a phone itself.

t007.text: And in its annual report to regulators, it wrote: our growth has stopped.

t008.text: Today's question: a company everyone says phones crushed, so how did its revenue double?

t009.text: I'm a Curio Files researcher; let's start at the top. Our first lead, Min Kao, was born in Zhushan, Taiwan.

t010.text: In 1971 he finished EE at NTU, then earned an EE PhD at Tennessee.

t011.text: He built navigation systems in the US, then satellite military navigation at a defense firm.

t012.text: Then, satellite positioning was a brand-new system. Who'd guess it would reach your car?

t013.text: Our second lead, Gary Burrell, ran several aircraft and marine electronics firms.

t014.text: Garmin says he designed the first successful nav/comm for small private planes.

t015.text: In 1983, Min Kao also joined an avionics company, and the two became colleagues. And then?

t016.text: In 1989 they started their own company, at first ProNav.

t017.text: Later renamed Garmin: Gary and Min, put together.

t020.text: Notice something? It still had nothing for your family car.

t021.text: So how did it get in?

t022.text: Per Wikipedia, its first portable car navigator came only in 1998.

t023.text: Problem was, satellite signals had a big flaw.

t024.text: The US deliberately added error to the civilian signal, citing national security.

t025.text: On May 1, 2000, the White House said the error would end at midnight.

t026.text: It said civilian accuracy could get up to 10x better.

t027.text: For a machine telling you to turn left here, I'd say that's huge.

t028.text: Six years later, in 2006, business exploded: company revenue jumped 73% in one go.

t031.text: The star was a line called nüvi.

t032.text: Auto was 28% of revenue in 2006, 52% the next year, 64% the year after.

t033.text: Picture it: of every $3, nearly $2 from one kind of device.

t034.text: It called its own factories in Xizhi, Zhongli and Linkou, Taiwan, a core strength.

t035.text: Selling like that, profits must have soared?

t036.text: Nope. The year nüvi hit 64%, it shipped 38% more units.

t038.text: The extra volume got eaten by price. It wrote: prices fell sharply over two years.

t039.text: Let me lay out that year's books.

t040.text: Of every $100 in car navigation, it kept just $38.50 after costs; aviation kept $67.

t041.text: So its best-selling navigator was its least profitable business.

t042.text: Revenue fell 14% that last quarter; it blamed the economy and the financial crisis.

t043.text: US-listed firms file an annual report each year with the US securities regulator, on business and risks.

t044.text: In February 2009, what did Garmin's report say under risks?

t045.text: It said: if phone navigation catches on, it could slow our growth.

t047.text: Its answer was blunt. Remember that phone?

t048.text: The same month, it announced an alliance with Taiwan's ASUS to co-brand phones.

t049.text: Unveiled a year earlier, nüvifone had calls, a browser, and navigation.

t050.text: See the move? If phones will steal navigation, make the phone yourself.

t051.text: Honestly, at first I thought: clever.

t052.text: It promised the first half; the first model only went on sale in Taiwan that July.

t053.text: One thing differed: this phone wasn't made in its own factories but by someone else.

t054.text: In October, a big US carrier signed on.

t055.text: But on the 28th that month, another company posted a blog entry.

t056.text: It was Google: Google Maps Navigation, for Android 2.0 phones.

t057.text: It had what a navigator has: voice guidance, 3D view, auto rerouting.

t058.text: And: never buy map updates again.

t060.text: Free. BBC noted rival phone navigation apps cost up to £60.

t061.text: That day Garmin's stock fell about 17%; BBC reported 18%.

t062.text: Holding its shares, you'd hardly sleep.

t063.text: A famous tech blogger wrote that day: dedicated navigators are nearly done.

t064.text: A finance site's headline asked if this was a category killer.

t065.text: I think "phones crushed navigators" began right about that day.

t066.text: Maybe you took yours down then.

t067.text: Four months later came the next annual report. Did "could" change?

t069.text: It also said several upcoming phones would run Google's Android.

t070.text: It tallied the prior year too: revenue down over 15%, auto down 19%.

t071.text: But note: auto units fell only 2%.

t072.text: What fell was price: the average down 18%.

t073.text: Aviation and marine fell too; it cited the economy.

t075.text: Free navigation came near year's end, so not all that drop is on phones.

t077.text: First, it gave up on its phone.

t078.text: In October 2010, it and ASUS said no new co-branded phones; the report just said: cancelled.

t079.text: That year auto revenue fell 19% again, under $1.7 billion.

t080.text: As boss, with 60% of income sliding, what would you write?

t081.text: On February 23, 2011, the report went in.

t082.text: Remember "our growth has stopped"? This was it.

t083.text: In the same sentence, "could slow" became "has caused our growth to stop."

t084.text: The next part added: this market has peaked.

t085.text: Note: its own account. The same report says more new cars offer navigation, and lists the economy as a risk.

t087.text: But that same day it also put out an earnings release.

t088.text: Its headline skipped navigators: outdoor, fitness, aviation and marine stay strong.

t091.text: Even counting deferred revenue back in, by my math they still earned over half.

t092.text: They didn't suddenly surge. Mainly auto's operating income fell from $520M to $250M in two years.

t093.text: Its segments then: auto was biggest, plus three small ones: outdoor and fitness, marine, and aviation.

t094.text: So when did those three small businesses start?

t095.text: Answer: always there. Remember those planes and boats?

t096.text: Back to 2003: Cessna picked its integrated avionics as standard on a new business jet.

t097.text: That November it began shipping a runner's device that measured speed, distance and laps by satellite.

t098.text: In 2003, your phone was maybe running Snake.

t099.text: So I don't call it a desperate pivot. My view:

t100.text: A phone rides along, but you won't wear it for a marathon,

t101.text: or wire it into a jet.

t102.text: Then the numbers moved: fitness grew 42% in 2010, 24% the next year.

t103.text: In July 2012, it launched its first GPS watch for hikers: fēnix.

t104.text: List price $399. Would you buy one?

t107.text: Company revenue stalled, down to about $2.6 billion in 2013.

t108.text: Auto's share of revenue fell from 58% to 19%.

t109.text: It topped its fiscal 2008 peak only in fiscal 2019, near $3.8 billion.

t112.text: Remember "over twice"? In fiscal 2025's $7.2 billion-plus, there's no piece called that 70%.

t113.text: Fitness, nearly a third; outdoor 28%; marine and aviation over 10% each. The smallest piece, under 10%.

t114.text: The story's not over. You may think: 70% down to under 10%, that's how auto vanished.

t115.text: The smallest supplies automakers: under 10%, and still losing money for the year.

t116.text: It makes systems built into new cars, not the old business renamed.

t118.text: Still sold; filed under outdoor, with no separate figure.

t119.text: Back around 2017: phone companies kept coming after fitness, too.

t120.text: The fiscal 2018 report lists fitness rivals: Apple, Samsung, Huawei.

t121.text: See? Several sell phones. The same rivals followed you to your wrist.

t122.text: It admitted that the year before, 2017, fitness revenue fell 7%, blaming a shrinking basic band market.

t124.text: Then in 2018 fitness grew 13% to become its biggest segment.

t127.text: Apple had 36% of shipments; Garmin, fifth.

t130.text: Latest: Q3 results out this October 28, revenue nearly $2 billion.

t131.text: Does that date ring a bell?

t132.text: Seventeen years ago, that free navigation post went up that day.

t133.text: Its own forecast: over $8.1B. Not yet real.

t134.text: So did Garmin ever beat phones at navigators?

t135.text: No. Phones stopped its growth: its own words, in its report.

t136.text: But per its own reports, phones weren't alone: built-in car nav, the economy and price wars too.

t137.text: Revenue doubled on business beyond the car: cockpits, boats, runners, and your wrist.

t138.text: My guess: had it bet only on car navigation, this file would likely stop at the 2011 page.

t140.text: Per its reports, phones did take a big chunk.

t141.text: But I think this file says: what got crushed was one business; what held the company up was the others it had started long before.

t143.text: Still got a navigator on your windshield? Tell me below.

t144.text: This channel covers only what's on record. To dig with us, subscribe.
